recent_posts.title: Introducing ARFBench: A time series question-answering benchmark based on real incidents
recent_posts.summary: ARFBench is a new time series question-answering benchmark derived from real production incidents at Datadog, consisting of 750 QA pairs across 63 incidents. It evaluates how well LLMs, vision-language models (VLMs), and time series foundation models (TSFMs) can perform observability tasks like anomaly identification and root cause localization. Key findings: GPT-5 leads existing models at 62.7% accuracy but still underperforms human domain experts; a new hybrid model combining Datadog's Toto TSFM with Qwen3-VL achieves comparable performance to frontier models with far fewer parameters; and a model-expert oracle combining AI and human judgment reaches 87.2% accuracy, establishing a new superhuman frontier. The benchmark and model weights are publicly available on Hugging Face.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: CMU researchers are presenting 194 papers at ICLR 2026 in Rio de Janeiro (April 23–27). The oral papers span topics including EditBench (a benchmark for LLM code editing), UALM (a unified audio language model), Agent Data Protocol (standardized training data for AI agents), MotionStream (real-time video generation), Mamba-3 (efficient sequence modeling), and hierarchical speculative decoding for faster LLM inference. Poster papers cover computer vision, deep learning, reinforcement learning, causal discovery, robotics, and AI safety/ethics. The breadth of work reflects CMU's research across LLM reasoning, multimodal models, embodied AI, and theoretical ML.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: LumberChunker is a document segmentation method that uses an LLM to detect semantic boundaries in long-form narrative text, producing more coherent chunks for RAG pipelines. Instead of fixed token windows or structural cues, it feeds rolling groups of paragraphs (around 550 tokens) to a language model and asks it to identify the earliest point where content meaningfully shifts. Evaluated on GutenQA—a new benchmark of 100 public-domain books with 3,000 retrieval questions—LumberChunker achieves DCG ≈ 62.1% and Recall ≈ 77.9% at k=20, outperforming semantic, recursive, paragraph-level, and proposition-level chunking methods. Downstream QA results show that focused retrieval with LumberChunker beats large-context non-retrieval setups and approaches human-curated segmentation quality.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: Carnegie Mellon researchers presented 156 papers at NeurIPS 2025 spanning diverse ML areas. Notable contributions include task-optimized neural networks for tactile processing that align with rodent brain activity, MeanFlow for one-step generative modeling achieving strong ImageNet results, and frameworks for computer-use agents and multi-agent collaboration. Research covers reinforcement learning scalability, LLM safety and alignment, speculative decoding optimization, vision-language models, and theoretical advances in game theory and causal inference. The work demonstrates CMU's breadth across foundational ML theory, practical systems, neuroscience-inspired models, and safety-critical applications.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: Researchers at Carnegie Mellon tested how major LLMs respond to age-sensitive questions like "Is Santa Claus real?" across different ages, languages, and contexts. They found significant variations: GPT-4o consistently says yes regardless of age, Claude tells the truth early (around age 6), while Gemini waits until teenage years. The study expanded to developmental milestones and World Values Survey questions, revealing that LLMs exhibit age-based and cultural biases in their responses. Language context dramatically affects answers—for example, GPT-4o tells French speakers to listen to parents until age 20 but Spanish speakers only until age 10. The research highlights how LLMs make invisible assumptions about user demographics and adjust responses accordingly, sometimes misaligning with actual cultural survey data.

recent_posts.title: Validating LLM-as-a-Judge Systems under Rating Indeterminacy
recent_posts.summary: A framework for validating LLM-as-a-judge systems when rating tasks have multiple correct answers (rating indeterminacy). The approach uses response set elicitation instead of forced-choice ratings, aggregates disagreement into multi-label vectors, and measures human-judge agreement with continuous metrics like MSE. Experiments across nine commercial LLMs and eleven rating tasks show that traditional forced-choice metrics select suboptimal judge systems, while the proposed multi-label approach correctly identifies high-performing judges for downstream tasks like content filtering and prevalence estimation.

Key contributions include task-optimized neural networks for tactile processing that align with rodent brain activity, MeanFlow for one-step generative modeling achieving strong image generation results, and frameworks for computer-use agents and multi-agent collaboration. Research spans reinforcement learning with horizon reduction for scalability, speculative decoding optimizations for LLM inference, safety benchmarks for AI agents, and methods for improving language model alignment through checklist-based feedback. Additional work addresses 3D scene understanding, speech quality evaluation, molecular property prediction, and data attribution in large language models.

recent_posts.title: How to Explore to Scale RL Training of LLMs on Hard Problems?
recent_posts.summary: Researchers at CMU introduce POPE (Privileged On-Policy Exploration), a method to scale reinforcement learning training of large language models on difficult problems. Current RL approaches plateau on hard problems because they rely on on-policy sampling that fails to discover correct solutions. POPE addresses this by conditioning models on prefixes of human solutions as guidance during training, enabling exploration in states where reward is more accessible. This guided exploration improves solvability by ~13% compared to standard approaches while avoiding optimization pathologies like entropy collapse. The method works through a stitching mechanism where instruction-following and reasoning capabilities allow models to transfer learning from guided to unguided problem variants.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: Carnegie Mellon University researchers are presenting 50 papers at EMNLP 2025, covering diverse NLP and ML topics including multimodal models, AI safety, reasoning capabilities, code generation, and human-AI interaction. The research spans theoretical advances in model interpretability and alignment, practical applications in chemistry and finance, and novel benchmarks for evaluating LLM performance across languages and domains. Key themes include inference-time scaling, retrieval-augmented generation, and interdisciplinary applications of language models.

recent_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
recent_posts.summary: BaNEL (Bayesian Negative Evidence Learning) is a novel algorithm that trains generative models using only failed attempts, addressing the challenge of extremely sparse rewards in hard problems like theorem proving and drug discovery. By learning patterns from failures through a separate generative model, BaNEL achieves up to 278x improvement in success rates while minimizing expensive reward evaluations. The approach trades compute for reward efficiency, demonstrating that machines can learn from negative evidence alone—similar to how human scientists generalize from past mistakes.

top_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
top_posts.summary: Copilot Arena is a Visual Studio Code extension designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) in real-world settings by collecting developer preferences during their actual workflow. The platform has gained over 11,000 users and supports numerous code completions and completion battles. It has shown insights into user preferences and how different models perform on various tasks. The evaluation highlights the importance of human feedback for performance metrics, contrasting with static benchmarks. Extensions to include more nuanced feedback mechanisms are encouraged.

top_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
top_posts.summary: Carnegie Mellon University researchers are presenting 127 papers at ICML 2025, covering diverse areas from game theory and differential privacy to large language models and computer vision. Notable contributions include new frameworks for adversarial environments, benchmarks for scientific equation discovery with LLMs, methods for improving AI safety and evaluation, and techniques for scaling test-time compute. The research spans theoretical advances in variational inequalities and online learning, practical applications in robotics and 3D object localization, and novel approaches to training more creative and curious AI agents.

top_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
top_posts.summary: State-of-the-art benchmarks for evaluating unlearning in large language models (LLMs) are flawed due to their separate evaluation of forget and retain queries, which do not account for potential dependencies. This makes it challenging to accurately measure progress in unlearning algorithms. Researchers highlight that these benchmarks might overestimate effectiveness and are potentially misleading. The study proposes improvements and introduces new datasets to address these issues, urging the community to develop more rigorous evaluation methods.

top_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
top_posts.summary: Recent research indicates that large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks, which can lead LLM-controlled robots to perform harmful actions in the physical world. Examples include robots used in self-driving cars, automated kitchens, and robot-assisted surgery. The post discusses various threat models and presents RoboPAIR, a new method for jailbreaking that is more effective than previous methods. Emphasis is placed on the need for robust defenses and the potential real-world risks posed by these vulnerabilities.

top_posts.title: Machine Learning Blog | ML@CMU | Carnegie Mellon University
top_posts.summary: Allie is a human-aligned AI chess bot developed by Carnegie Mellon University, designed to play chess in a way that feels natural and matches the skill levels of human players. Unlike traditional chess engines, Allie uses a Transformer model trained on game transcripts and adapts its play style to mimic human behavior, including pondering time and move choices. It employs adaptive Monte-Carlo Tree Search to vary its search depth based on the complexity of positions, aiming to provide a more human-like chess experience. Despite progress, there are still areas for improvement, particularly in modeling human reasoning in longer games.
